title: Generalized implementation of invariant coordinate selection with positive semi-definite scatter matrices
Generalized implementation of invariant coordinate selection with positive semi-definite scatter matrices
summary: Classical invariant coordinate selection (ICS) requires two positive definite scatter matrices and becomes unsolvable when collinearity makes at least one scatter matrix singular. The paper proposes and studies three generalizations: a Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse approach, a dimension-reduction preprocessing approach, and a generalized singular value decomposition approach. Theoretically and empirically, GSVD appears most promising because it preserves affine invariance, treats V1 and V2 symmetrically, and can recover structure in null-space directions, whereas GINV and DR have important limitations.

A 10% relative band is used around the finite target ρ=1 (absolute ±0.1); for the companion zero eigenvalues, the same absolute 0.1 band is used because a relative band at zero is undefined.

why: The authors released the R scripts and an renv.lock for the illustrative example. Claims C1/C2 require only a 4x4 generalized eigenproblem from a self-contained simulated example; no external data or weights are needed. The only likely setup is installing R and restoring the declared CRAN packages.
est_runtime: Seconds for the 4x4 eigenproblem once R and packages are installed; first-time R/package setup may take several minutes.
blockers: The machine has Python but no R runtime listed; this is an R-only repository requiring R 4.3.3 and CRAN packages declared in renv.lock.
First run may require renv::restore(); package installation is the main setup cost, not the computation.

approach: Use the authors' repository as the reference implementation, but make the entrypoint Python-only because the sandbox exposes no R runtime and only Python, pip, and git can be executed. For the matched claim C1/C2, the exact target is deterministic: reconstruct the theoretical scatter functionals V1=diag(I2,0) and V2=diag(I2, epsilon*diag(2,0)) with epsilon=20/1000, form V1^+ V2 using a spectral Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse, and report the sorted eigenvalues. The simulation with n=1000 and exactly 20 outliers is generated only as a sample-level sanity check and optional plotting input; the exact 1,1,0,0 result comes from the theoretical matrices and is seed-independent. If Rscript happens to be available, reproduce.py will also invoke the authors' illustrative-example script for artifact generation, but it will never depend on R for results/metrics.json.
steps: Clone or verify the authors' repository at https://github.com/AuroreAA/ICS_PSD_Replication into ./repo; confirm code/ICS_PSD_illustrative_example.R, code/ICS_PSD_illustrative_example_G.R, code/utilities.R, and renv.lock exist.
Create results/ and results/figures/; keep all generated outputs out of the cloned repository.
Implement src/config.py with the exact constants from the claim contract, especially n=1000, n_outliers=20, p=4, W1=I2, W2=diag(2,0), and epsilon=20/1000.

Implement src/ginv.py: (a) eigendecompose V1 with numpy.linalg.eigh; (b) retain eigenvalues greater than the configured rank tolerance; (c) build V1^+ = U diag(1/lambda_r) U^T; (d) form M = V1^+ @ V2; (e) use numpy.linalg.eig for the non-symmetric EVP; (f) discard numerical imaginary parts smaller than 1e-12 and sort real eigenvalues descending.

Implement src/simulate.py: create an n x p sample with first 980 rows from N(0, diag(W1,0)) and last 20 rows from N(0, diag(W1, 2, 0)); use the fixed seed; assert exactly 20 outliers and shape (1000,4).

Implement src/rank_criteria.py as an optional diagnostic only: compute SVD singular values and relative rank criteria lambda_i/lambda_1 < sqrt(nu), < max(n,p)*nu, and cumulative squared eigenvalues < 0.99; do not use it for the C1/C2 pass/fail.

Implement src/author_runner.py: use shutil.which('Rscript'); if found, run the authors' illustrative-example R script from the repository root and capture stdout/stderr; if not found, record 'R unavailable; Python equivalent used' in the log and continue.

Implement reproduce.py: load config, build theoretical V1 and V2, compute GINV eigenvalues, assert four eigenvalues, assert sorted descending, assert ranks rank(V1)=2 and rank(V2)=3, and compare to expected [1,1,0,0] with the configured C1/C2 tolerances.
In reproduce.py, compute pass_C1 = abs(rho1 - 1.0) <= 0.1 and abs(rho2 - 1.0) <= 0.1; compute pass_C2 = abs(rho3) <= 0.1 and abs(rho4) <= 0.1; overall pass is pass_C1 and pass_C2.

Write results/metrics.json containing claim_id, status, method, V1, V2, V1_pinv, V1_pinv_V2, eigenvalues, expected_eigenvalues, tolerance, pass flags, R_script_status, and the null-space limitation note from Remark 1.
Run the smoke mode first, then the full entrypoint: `python reproduce.py --smoke` followed by `python reproduce.py`.
Open results/metrics.json and verify the computed eigenvalues are numerically [1,1,0,0] (or within machine precision) and that the overall pass flag is true.
smoke_test: Run `python reproduce.py --smoke`. This constructs only the 4x4 theoretical V1 and V2, prints their shapes, ranks, V1^+ V2 matrix, and eigenvalues, and asserts that the sorted eigenvalues match [1,1,0,0] within 1e-12. It exercises the exact data flow used for C1/C2 without generating the full simulation.
intermediate_checks: Assert V1 shape is (4,4), V2 shape is (4,4), and both are symmetric.
Assert rank(V1) = 2 and rank(V2) = 3 for the theoretical matrices.
Assert V1^+ V2 equals diag(1,1,0,0) up to machine precision.
Assert the four GINV eigenvalues are real up to 1e-12 and sorted in descending order.
Check that the first two eigenvalues are 1 and the last two are 0 within machine precision before applying the 0.1 tolerance.
For the optional simulation, assert the generated sample has shape (1000,4), exactly 20 outlier rows, and no NaN values.
Check that Rscript is either found or explicitly reported as unavailable; the metric must not depend on R.
Confirm metrics.json contains both C1 and C2 companion values, not only a single aggregate number.
budget_plan: Total budget ~15 minutes. Setup and repository inspection: 4 minutes. Implement config, GINV, simulation, and reproduce.py: 4 minutes. Smoke test: 1 minute. Full run and metrics.json inspection: 1 minute. Buffer for environment/JSON checks and optional author R invocation attempt: 5 minutes. The numerical computation itself is under 1 second; the budget is dominated by setup and verification.

=== page 1 ===
Generalized implementation of invariant coordinate selection with positive
semi-definite scatter matrices
Aurore Archimbauda
aTBS Business School, 1 Place Alphonse Jourdain, 31000 Toulouse, France
Abstract
Invariant coordinate selection is an unsupervised multivariate data transformation useful in many contexts such as
outlier detection or clustering. It is based on the simultaneous diagonalization of two affine equivariant and positive
definite scatter matrices. Its classical implementation relies on a non-symmetric eigenvalue problem by diagonalizing
one scatter relatively to the other. In case of collinearity, at least one of the scatter matrices is singular, making
the problem unsolvable. To address this limitation, three approaches are proposed using: a Moore-Penrose pseudo
inverse, a dimension reduction, and a generalized singular value decomposition. Their properties are investigated both
theoretically and through various empirical applications. Overall, the extension based on the generalized singular
value decomposition seems the most promising, even though it restricts the choice of scatter matrices to those that
can be expressed as cross-products. In practice, some of the approaches also appear suitable in the context of data in
high-dimension low-sample-size data.
Keywords: Dimension reduction, Generalized Eigenvalue Problem, High-dimension, Pseudo-inverse, Singular
scatters, Singular value decomposition

4. Empirical applications
In this section, we illustrate the characteristics of the different approaches on different empirical applications. We
restrict our analysis to ICS with a generalized inverse (GINV), pre-processed by a dimension reduction (DR) through

a singular value decomposition and using the generalized value decomposition (GSVD). We exclude the direct GEP
approach since it might result in complex and negative eigenvalues. First, Subsection 4.1 analyses the consequences
of exchanging the role of V1 and V2 on a simulated correlated mixture of Gaussian distributions. Subsection 4.2
focuses on two examples for which estimating the rank of the data is challenging. Subsection 4.3 evaluates the impact
of transforming the data through an affine transformation on a collinear industrial data set. Finally, Subsection 4.4
investigates if those approaches are applicable also in case of high dimension low sample size (HDLSS) with n < p.

4.1. Comparison of the three approaches: collinear clustering application
Let X = (X1, . . . , Xd)⊤be a d-variate real random vector distributed according to a mixture of two Gaussian
distributions such that:
X ∼ε1 N(μ1, Id) + ε2 N(μ2, Id),
(13)
with ε1 + ε2 = 1, μ1 = 0d, μ2 = (δ, 0, . . . , 0)⊤where δ = 10. We generate n = 1000 observations on d = 3 variables for
two balanced groups with ε1 = ε2 = 0.5. Two collinear variables are added: X4 = X2 −3X3 and X5 = X3 + 5X4.
4.1.1. COV-COV4
First of all, we compare the different ICS methods for the scatter pair COV −COV4. For GSVD, we consider
GCOV4 since it is not possible to compute COV4(Xn) as Xn is not full rank and so COV(Xn) is singular and it
cannot be inverted. Figure 4 shows the scatterplots matrix of the IC resulting of ICS with the generalized inverse of
COV (GINV on 1st column), after a dimension reduction (DR on 2nd column) and with a generalized singular value
decomposition (GSVD on 3rd column). The second row illustrates the same results when we exchange V1 and V2.
It is interesting to note that depending on the method we do not obtain the same number of components: 5 with
GINV and 3 for the other two. Indeed, with a DR the rank of the data is estimated to be 3 and so only three dimensions
are kept. For GSVD, three non-trivial eigenvalues are also detected. For GINV, 5 components are illustrated but the
last two are associated with almost zero eigenvalues: 1.5e−15 and −2.5e−18. Clearly, this indicates numerical issues
and the last two components should be disregarded. Now, if we focus on the first three, we can notice that all the
methods allow us to easily identify the two clusters on IC3. In addition, the components are the same between GINV
and DR as mentioned in Property 3. Finally, if we exchange V1 and V2 then the clustering structure is shown on the
first component for the three methods. So here, on an example of simple collinearity it appears that the three methods
lead to similar results. The only point of attention is with GINV, where some trivial eigenvalues are estimated and
should be put away.

    3| ## About ICS
    4| Invariant Coordinate Selection (ICS) is a powerful unsupervised multivariate method designed to identify the structure of multivariate datasets on a subspace. """Single source of truth for the illustrative GINV example (Section 2.3, Example 1).

All constants come from the paper (arXiv:2409.02258) or from the assumption ledger
(state/assumption_ledger.json).  Nothing here is a *result*: the eigenvalues reported
in results/metrics.json are computed by src/ginv.py from these inputs only.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import os

import numpy as np

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- data model --
# Section 2.3 / requirement R3, R4: p = 4, W1 = I2, W2 = diag(2, 0),
# n = 1000 observations with exactly 20 outliers.
N_OBS = 1000
N_OUTLIERS = 20
P_DIM = 4                       # A1: W1 is 2x2 and W2 is 2x2 -> p = 4
EPSILON = N_OUTLIERS / N_OBS    # A5: eps = 20/1000 = 0.02

W1 = np.eye(2)                            # R3
W2 = np.diag([2.0, 0.0])                  # R3

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- scatter ----
# R5: the exact eigenvalue check uses the *theoretical* scatter functionals,
#   V1 = diag(W1, 0)          ("perfectly robust", singular, rank 2)
#   V2 = diag(W1, eps * W2)   (covariance of the whole mixture)
# Block layout follows A6: the third coordinate carries W2's variance 2,
# the fourth carries W2's variance 0.


def block_diag(top: np.ndarray, bottom: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    out = np.zeros((top.shape[0] + bottom.shape[0], top.shape[1] + bottom.shape[1]))
    out[: top.shape[0], : top.shape[1]] = top
    out[top.shape[0]:, top.shape[1]:] = bottom
    return out


V1_THEORETICAL = block_diag(W1, np.zeros((2, 2)))            # diag(1, 1, 0, 0)
V2_THEORETICAL = block_diag(W1, EPSILON * W2)                # diag(1, 1, 0.04, 0)

# Example 2 (R9): the affine counterexample applies the p x p Toeplitz matrix A
# of Section 2.3 (first column (1, 1/p, ..., (p-1)/p)); the authors' replication
# script uses G = toeplitz(p:1)/p, which is the same symmetric matrix.
TOEPLITZ_A = np.array(
    [[max(P_DIM - abs(i - j), 1) for j in range(P_DIM)] for i in range(P_DIM)]
) / float(P_DIM)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- GINV ------
# R1/R2: V1 is replaced by its Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse built from the
# spectral decomposition, keeping only the r1 non-zero eigenvalues.
# A7: pseudo-inverse rank tolerance.  The authors' R helper mat_sqrt_ginv()
# keeps eigenvalues > tolerance * lambda_max with tolerance = .Machine$double.eps;
# we use the same relative rule with a slightly larger, documented cut-off.
PINV_REL_TOL = float(np.finfo(float).eps)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- targets ---
# C1: rho1 = rho2 = 1 ; C2: rho3 = rho4 = 0 (Example 1, Figure 2 left panel).
EXPECTED_EIGENVALUES = np.array([1.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0])
TOL_UNIT = 0.1        # claim contract: relative 0.1 for the finite target rho = 1
TOL_ZERO = 0.1        # claim contract: absolute 0.1 for the zero companion eigenvalues
IMAG_TOL = 1e-12      # A10: eigenvalues are real up to this numerical imaginary part

SEED = 12345          # A4: fixed seed, used only for the optional sample sanity check

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- paths -----
RESULTS_DIR = os.path.join("results")
FIGURES_DIR = os.path.join(RESULTS_DIR, "figures")
METRICS_PATH = os.path.join(RESULTS_DIR, "metrics.json")

REMARK1_LIMITATION = (
    "GINV with the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse only searches the range space of V1 "
    "(Remark 1 / R7): directions b in null(V1) - null(V2), where the outlier structure "
    "of W2 lives (here the 3rd coordinate, variance eps*2 in V2), are not recoverable. "
    "The exact GEP V2 b = rho V1 b would give rho = inf for such a direction, but "
    "V1^+ V2 collapses it to rho = 0, so the reported eigenvalues are 1, 1, 0, 0 and "
    "the informative outlier direction is lost. The roles of V1 and V2 are not "
    "exchangeable (R6); V1 is the singular matrix whose pseudo-inverse is taken."
)

"""GINV: ICS with a positive semi-definite V1 handled by the Moore-Penrose
pseudo-inverse (paper Section 3.1, Eq. (7)).

Requirements implemented
------------------------
R1  solve V1^+ V2 b = rho b instead of V1^{-1} V2 b = rho b when V1 is singular.
R2  V1^+ is built from the spectral decomposition of V1, inverting only the r1
    non-zero eigenvalues (Lambda_{r1}^{-1}).
R6  the roles of V1 and V2 are asymmetric: V1 is the matrix that is pseudo-inverted.
R8  all p eigenvalues are returned (two equal to one, two equal to zero here).
R7  the null-space limitation is exposed as a diagnostic (see remark1_diagnostics).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass

import numpy as np


def spectral_pinv(V: np.ndarray, rel_tol: float) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray, int]:
    """Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse of a symmetric PSD matrix from its spectrum.

    Returns (V_pinv, eigenvalues, eigenvectors_kept, r1).  Zero eigenvalues are
    *not* inverted (R2): only the r1 eigenvalues above rel_tol * lambda_max are kept.
    """
    V = np.asarray(V, dtype=float)
    values, vectors = np.linalg.eigh(V)          # ascending, real (symmetric input)
    values = values[::-1]
    vectors = vectors[:, ::-1]                   # descending order
    lam_max = values[0] if values.size else 0.0
    keep = values > rel_tol * lam_max
    r1 = int(np.count_nonzero(keep))
    if r1 == 0:
        return np.zeros_like(V), values, vectors, 0
    U = vectors[:, keep]
    lam = values[keep]
    V_pinv = (U / lam) @ U.T                     # U diag(1/lam) U'
    return 0.5 * (V_pinv + V_pinv.T), values, vectors, r1


def spectral_pinv_sqrt(V: np.ndarray, rel_tol: float) -> np.ndarray:
    """V1^{-1/2} restricted to the range space (the authors' mat_sqrt_ginv helper)."""
    V = np.asarray(V, dtype=float)
    values, vectors = np.linalg.eigh(V)
    values = values[::-1]
    vectors = vectors[:, ::-1]
    lam_max = values[0] if values.size else 0.0
    keep = values > rel_tol * lam_max
    if np.count_nonzero(keep) == 0:
        return np.zeros_like(V)
    U = vectors[:, keep]
    lam = values[keep]
    W = (U / np.sqrt(lam)) @ U.T                 # U diag(1/sqrt(lam)) U'
    return 0.5 * (W + W.T)


@dataclass
class GinvResult:
    eigenvalues: np.ndarray      # all p eigenvalues, sorted descending (A8)
    matrix: np.ndarray           # V1^+ V2 (non-symmetric operator of Eq. (7))
    r1: int                      # numerical rank of V1
    imaginary_max: float         # largest |Im| before discarding
    symmetric_eigenvalues: np.ndarray  # eigenvalues of V1^{-1/2} V2 V1^{-1/2}


def ginv_eigenvalues(V1: np.ndarray, V2: np.ndarray, rel_tol: float) -> GinvResult:
    """Solve the GINV eigenvalue problem V1^+ V2 b = rho b (R1) and return all p rho.

    Two equivalent routes are computed and both are reported:
      * the non-symmetric EVP for M = V1^+ V2 (Eq. (7), A10), and
      * the symmetric EVP for V1^{-1/2} V2 V1^{-1/2}, which is what the authors'
        R helper ICS_ginv(algorithm = "standard") diagonalises.
    """
    V1 = np.asarray(V1, dtype=float)
    V2 = np.asarray(V2, dtype=float)
    V1_pinv, _, _, r1 = spectral_pinv(V1, rel_tol)
    M = V1_pinv @ V2

    raw = np.linalg.eigvals(M)
    imag_max = float(np.max(np.abs(raw.imag))) if raw.size else 0.0
    if imag_max > 1e-6:
        raise ValueError(f"GINV eigenvalues have a large imaginary part ({imag_max:g})")
    rho = np.sort(np.real_if_close(raw, tol=1000).real)[::-1]      # descending (A8)

    W = spectral_pinv_sqrt(V1, rel_tol)
    rho_sym = np.sort(np.linalg.eigvalsh(W @ V2 @ W))[::-1]

    return GinvResult(
        eigenvalues=rho,
        matrix=M,
        r1=r1,
        imaginary_max=imag_max,
        symmetric_eigenvalues=rho_sym,
    )


def remark1_diagnostics(V1: np.ndarray, V2: np.ndarray, rel_tol: float) -> dict:
    """R7: report the directions in null(V1) - null(V2) that GINV cannot recover."""
    _, _, _, r1 = spectral_pinv(V1, rel_tol)
    null_V1 = np.linalg.matrix_rank(V1, tol=rel_tol * np.linalg.eigvalsh(V1)[-1])
    null_V1 = V1.shape[0] - r1
    null_V2 = V2.shape[0] - np.linalg.matrix_rank(V2)

    # exact GEP V2 b = rho V1 b: rho = inf iff b in null(V1) but V2 b != 0

#!/usr/bin/env python
"""Reproduce the matched claim C1/C2 of arXiv:2409.02258.

Target (Example 1, Section 2.3 / 3.1, Figure 2 left panel):
    ICS with the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse of the singular scatter matrix V1
    applied to W1 = I2, W2 = diag(2, 0), p = 4, n = 1000 with exactly 20 outliers
    yields the eigenvalue pattern rho1 = rho2 = 1 and rho3 = rho4 = 0.

Everything in results/metrics.json is computed here from the paper's *inputs*
(W1, W2, n, number of outliers); no result number is typed in.

Usage:
    python reproduce.py            # full run (writes results/metrics.json)
    python reproduce.py --smoke    # 4x4 theoretical eigenproblem only
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys

import numpy as np

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))

from src import config
from src.ginv import ginv_eigenvalues, remark1_diagnostics, spectral_pinv


def _rank(M: np.ndarray) -> int:
    return int(np.linalg.matrix_rank(M))


def theoretical_check() -> dict:
    """C1/C2: GINV eigenvalues of the theoretical scatter functionals V1, V2."""
    V1, V2 = config.V1_THEORETICAL, config.V2_THEORETICAL
    assert V1.shape == (config.P_DIM, config.P_DIM) == V2.shape
    assert np.allclose(V1, V1.T) and np.allclose(V2, V2.T)

    res = ginv_eigenvalues(V1, V2, config.PINV_REL_TOL)
    rho = res.eigenvalues
    assert rho.shape == (config.P_DIM,), rho
    assert np.all(np.diff(rho) <= 1e-12), "eigenvalues must be sorted descending"
    assert res.imaginary_max < config.IMAG_TOL, res.imaginary_max
    assert _rank(V1) == 2, _rank(V1)
    assert _rank(V2) == 3, _rank(V2)

    V1_pinv, _, _, r1 = spectral_pinv(V1, config.PINV_REL_TOL)
    assert r1 == 2
    # V1^+ V2 = diag(1, 1, 0, 0) for this example
    assert np.allclose(res.matrix, np.diag([1.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0]), atol=1e-12), res.matrix

    rho1, rho2, rho3, rho4 = (float(v) for v in rho)
    pass_c1 = abs(rho1 - 1.0) <= config.TOL_UNIT and abs(rho2 - 1.0) <= config.TOL_UNIT
    pass_c2 = abs(rho3) <= config.TOL_ZERO and abs(rho4) <= config.TOL_ZERO

    return {
        "rho": rho,
        "rho1": rho1,
        "rho2": rho2,
        "rho3": rho3,
        "rho4": rho4,
        "rho_symmetric": res.symmetric_eigenvalues,
        "matrix": res.matrix,
        "V1_pinv": V1_pinv,
        "r1": r1,
        "pass_C1": bool(pass_c1),
        "pass_C2": bool(pass_c2),
        "diagnostics": remark1_diagnostics(V1, V2, config.PINV_REL_TOL),
    }


def affine_check() -> dict:
    """Example 2 / R9: GINV eigenvalues after the Toeplitz transformation X* = A X."""
    A = config.TOEPLITZ_A
    V1 = A @ config.V1_THEORETICAL @ A.T
    V2 = A @ config.V2_THEORETICAL @ A.T
    res = ginv_eigenvalues(V1, V2, config.PINV_REL_TOL)
    return {"eigenvalues": res.eigenvalues, "r1": res.r1, "A": A}


def sample_sanity_check() -> dict:
    """R4: generate n = 1000 observations with exactly 20 outliers (seeded, optional)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(config.SEED)
    n, k = config.N_OBS, config.N_OUTLIERS
    normal = rng.standard_normal((n - k, config.P_DIM))
    normal[:, 2:] *= 0.0                                  # N(0, diag(W1, 0))
    out = rng.standard_normal((k, config.P_DIM))
    out[:, 2:] *= np.sqrt(np.diag(config.W2)) * np.sqrt(config.EPSILON)
    X = np.vstack([normal, out])
    assert X.shape == (n, config.P_DIM)
    assert not np.isnan(X).any()
    return {"shape": X.shape, "n_outliers": k}


def author_r_status() -> str:
    """R11: the authors' scripts are R; Rscript is not available in this sandbox."""
    rscript = shutil.which("Rscript")
    if not rscript:
        return "Rscript not on PATH; Python equivalent used for all reported numbers"
    try:
        p = subprocess.run([rscript, "--version"], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=30)
        return f"Rscript found: {p.stdout.strip() or p.stderr.strip()}"
    except Exception as exc:  # pragma: no cover
        return f"Rscript found but not runnable: {exc}"


def main(smoke: bool = False) -> int:
    os.makedirs(config.RESULTS_DIR, exist_ok=True)
    chk = theoretical_check()
    rho = chk["rho"]
    print("V1 =", config.V1_THEORETICAL.tolist())
    print("V2 =", config.V2_THEORETICAL.tolist())
    print("rank(V1) =", _rank(config.V1_THEORETICAL), " rank(V2) =", _rank(config.V2_THEORETICAL))
    print("V1^+ V2 =", np.round(chk["matrix"], 12).tolist())
    print("GINV eigenvalues (V1^+V2)        =", rho)
    print("GINV eigenvalues (V1^-1/2 V2 ...)=", chk["rho_symmetric"])
    print("C1 (rho1=rho2=1):", chk["pass_C1"], " C2 (rho3=rho4=0):", chk["pass_C2"])
    print("Remark 1 diagnostic:", chk["diagnostics"])

    if smoke:

        print("smoke OK: eigenvalues match [1, 1, 0, 0] within 1e-12")
        return 0

    extra = affine_check()
    sample = sample_sanity_check()
    r_status = author_r_status()
    print("affine-transformed GINV eigenvalues =", extra["eigenvalues"])
    print("sample shape =", sample["shape"], "outliers =", sample["n_outliers"])

        "value": float(rho[1]),
        "dataset": "Simulated Gaussian mixture from Section 2.3 "

            "W2": config.W2.tolist(),
            "V1": config.V1_THEORETICAL.tolist(),

"""Optional cross-check of the GINV eigenvalues with the paper's own language (R).

The authors' replication script (repo/code/ICS_PSD_illustrative_example.R) needs the
CRAN packages ICSOutlier / ICSClust / geigen / rrcov, which are not installed in this
sandbox, so it cannot be executed as-is.  What *can* be executed with a bare R
installation is the numerical core of their helper chain:

    W1 <- mat_sqrt_ginv(V1, inverse = TRUE, tolerance = .Machine$double.eps)
    eigen(W1 %*% V2 %*% W1, symmetric = TRUE)$values

which is exactly the pseudo-inverse GINV route of Section 3.1 (R1/R2).  This module
writes that base-R snippet, runs it if an Rscript binary can be found, and returns
its eigenvalues.  Nothing here is required for the reported metric: every failure is
caught and reported as a status string, and results/metrics.json is always produced
by the Python implementation in src/ginv.py.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import glob
import os
import shutil
import subprocess

R_SNIPPET = """\
mat_sqrt_ginv <- function(A, inverse = TRUE, tolerance = .Machine$double.eps) {
  eigen_A <- eigen(A, symmetric = TRUE)
  r1 <- which(eigen_A$values > max(tolerance * eigen_A$values[1]))
  if (isTRUE(inverse)) {
    tcrossprod(sweep(eigen_A$vectors[, r1, drop = FALSE], 2, 1 / sqrt(eigen_A$values[r1]), "*"))
  } else {
    tcrossprod(sweep(eigen_A$vectors[, r1, drop = FALSE], 2, sqrt(eigen_A$values[r1]), "*"))

def find_rscript() -> str | None:
    p = shutil.which("Rscript")
    if p:
        return p
    candidates: list[str] = []
    for pattern in (
        r"C:/Program Files/R/*/bin/Rscript.exe",
        r"C:/Program Files/R/*/bin/x64/Rscript.exe",
        os.path.expanduser(r"~/AppData/Local/Programs/R/*/bin/Rscript.exe"),
    ):
        candidates.extend(glob.glob(pattern))
    return sorted(candidates)[-1] if candidates else None


def run_r_cross_check(work_dir: str, timeout: int = 90) -> tuple[str, list[float] | None]:
    """Return (status_string, eigenvalues or None). Never raises."""
    rscript = find_rscript()
    if not rscript:
        return "R not available in this sandbox; authors' R script not executed", None
    try:
        os.makedirs(work_dir, exist_ok=True)
        path = os.path.join(work_dir, "ginv_baseR_check.R")
        with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
            fh.write(R_SNIPPET)
        proc = subprocess.run([rscript, path], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout)
        if proc.returncode != 0:
            return f"R cross-check failed ({rscript}): {proc.stderr.strip()[:200]}", None
        vals = [float(line) for line in proc.stdout.split() if line.strip()]
        if len(vals) != 4:
            return f"R cross-check returned {len(vals)} values, expected 4", None
        return f"base-R cross-check with {rscript} (authors' mat_sqrt_ginv logic)", vals
    except Exception as exc:  # pragma: no cover - defensive
        return f"R cross-check skipped: {exc}", None

target.statement: In the illustrative simulation with W1=I2 and W2=diag(2,0), ICS using the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse of V1 yields two unit eigenvalues: ρ1=ρ2=1.
target.unit: eigenvalue (dimensionless); companion claim C2 gives ρ3=ρ4=0
target.dataset: Simulated Gaussian mixture from Section 2.3 (n=1000, 20 outliers, p=4, W1=I2, W2=diag(2,0))

tolerance.why: Rule 4: no standard deviation is reported, the target is not a bounded accuracy-like score, and eigenvalues are unbounded. A 10% relative band is used around the finite target ρ=1 (absolute ±0.1); for the companion zero eigenvalues, the same absolute 0.1 band is used because a relative band at zero is undefined.

audit_summary: The matched C1/C2 target is reproduced exactly: the code builds V1=diag(1,1,0,0) and V2=diag(1,1,0.04,0), forms the spectral Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse with r1=2, solves V1^+V2, and obtains [1,1,0,0] on a clean rerun (exit 0, about 1 s). This is the paper's specified theoretical-scatter configuration for Example 1, not a sample-estimate substitute, so the experiment is right. R1/R2/R5/R6 are faithfully implemented, R7's null-space limitation is reported, and the extra R9 affine check gives the expected non-invariant pattern [1.1237,1,~0,~0]. Expected target values appear in config only for pass/assert comparisons; the reported metric value and eigenvalue vector are computed from the scatter matrices, so I found no anti-cheat violation. The main gaps are outside the C1 target: GSVD (R10), DR rank criteria (R12), and the full R 4.3.3/CRAN package chain (R11) are not implemented, and the non-target GSVD/HTP claims are not reproduced. No scale-down applies to the run that produced the C1 value.

requirement_check.evidence: src/ginv.py::ginv_eigenvalues builds M = V1_pinv @ V2 and computes np.linalg.eigvals(M), i.e. the GINV EVP V1^+ V2 b = rho b. The clean re-run reports V1^+V2 = diag(1,1,0,0) and eigenvalues [1,1,0,0].
src/ginv.py::spectral_pinv uses np.linalg.eigh, keeps only values > rel_tol*lambda_max, forms V_pinv=(U/lam)@U.T, and returns r1=2 for V1=diag(1,1,0,0); zero eigenvalues are not inverted.
src/config.py sets P_DIM=4, W1=np.eye(2), W2=np.diag([2.0,0.0]), and constructs V1/V2 as the corresponding 4x4 block matrices.

src/reproduce.py::sample_sanity_check generates n=1000 rows with exactly 20 outlier rows and asserts shape (1000,4) and n_outliers=20; this sample is a sanity check only because R5 specifies theoretical scatter matrices for the exact eigenvalue target.
src/config.py defines V1_THEORETICAL=diag(W1,0)=diag(1,1,0,0) and V2_THEORETICAL=diag(W1,EPSILON*W2)=diag(1,1,0.04,0), with EPSILON=20/1000; theoretical_check uses exactly these matrices.
The GINV operator is formed as M = V1_pinv @ V2; only V1 is pseudo-inverted and V2 is not swapped. metrics.json states the same asymmetric-role configuration.

metrics.json contains null_space_limitation, and src/ginv.py::remark1_diagnostics identifies one direction in null(V1) minus null(V2) (the third coordinate) whose exact GEP eigenvalue is infinite but which GINV collapses to rho=0.
theoretical_check returns the full sorted vector rho of length p=4; metrics.json reports eigenvalues [1.0,1.0,0.0,0.0] with rho1=rho2=1 and rho3=rho4=0.

src/reproduce.py::affine_check applies the Section 2.3 Toeplitz matrix A to V1 and V2 and computes GINV eigenvalues [1.1236623, 1.0, 1.07e-17, -2.74e-16], confirming that the exact 1,1,0,0 pattern is lost under the affine transformation.

No GSVD implementation is present in reproduce.py or src/. The final code does not construct cross-product matrices XV1 and XV2 or solve the GSVD relation beta_i^2 V2 b_i = alpha_i^2 V1 b_i; command-ledger scipy.gsvd/qz attempts were exploratory and are not in the reproduced code.

The reported numbers come from a Python/numpy equivalent, and an optional base-R cross-check of the mat_sqrt_ginv pseudo-inverse core was run with R 4.6.1. The paper's full R 4.3.3 plus CRAN package chain (ICS, ICSClust, ICSOutlier, rrcov, geigen) was not installed or executed.

No DR/rank-criterion implementation appears in the final reproduce.py or src/ code, and the clean re-run does not compute or report the HTP2/HTP3 SVD rank criteria. Command-ledger HTP/SVD exploration was not carried into the reproduced result.
